title: The stupas
hookLine: Sanchi and Bharhut: great mounds holding relics, walked around clockwise

lines: A DOME LIKE AN UPTURNED BOWL.
cards: A dome of brick and stone, rounded like an upturned bowl, rises from a hilltop in central India.
Around it runs a stone railing, and through the railing, carved gateways crowded with elephants, trees and people, whole stories in relief. Pilgrims don't go inside. There is no inside to go to.
They walk around it, slowly, always in the same direction. This is the great stupa at Sanchi. Today's word is the shape itself.

teach.h: A MOUND WHERE FOUR ROADS MEET.
teach.b: First, the Buddha's own instruction. In the Great Discourse on the final passing, Ananda asks what should be done with the Teacher's body.
Treat it like the remains of a great king, the Buddha answers, and build a stupa where four roads meet.
Whoever brings a garland or scent there, or bows, or simply grows calm in heart, it will be for their good and happiness for a long time.
Second, the relics shared. After the cremation, the discourse says, the peoples who had loved him each asked for a share of the remains and built a stupa over theirs.
So from the start, a stupa is a mound with something precious sealed at its heart, out of sight. Third, Sanchi and Bharhut.
Their stone railings and gateways survive, covered with carvings: the Jataka tales, scenes from the Buddha's life, spirits of the trees, ordinary people bringing offerings.
Some carvings carry the names of those who paid for them, monks, nuns, merchants, villagers, their small gifts cut into the stone. Fourth, walking around it.
Pilgrims circle a stupa keeping it on their right, which means clockwise, an old Indian gesture of respect. In the suttas, visitors often leave the Buddha the same way, keeping him on their right.

At a stupa, the whole visit is that gesture, again and again. The body moves; the center stays still. And the walk becomes the prayer, or the meditation, or simply a way of saying: this matters, and I came.

how: At stupas and pagodas, Buddhist pilgrims walk clockwise, sometimes three times, sometimes chanting or carrying flowers and incense, as an act of respect and meditation.

games.q: walk around it: tap the pairs.
p: a mound with relics at its heart
where the Buddha said to build one

s: pilgrims go inside a stupa to pray
a stupa is a solid mound; pilgrims walk around it.
the Buddha himself spoke of building a stupa for his remains
in the Great Discourse on the final passing he tells Ananda to build one where four roads meet.
the carvings at Sanchi and Bharhut name only kings
some name the people who paid for them: monks, nuns, merchants, villagers.

games.q: you've traveled for days to reach a great stupa. you're standing at its gate. what do you do?
o: look for the door to go inside.
walk around it, keeping it on your right.
climb to the top for the view.
games.why: pilgrims circle the stupa clockwise, keeping it on their right, the same gesture people in the suttas make when they leave the Buddha.

practice: Choose something near you, a table, a chair, a plant, and walk slowly around it once, keeping it on your right and feeling each foot land; if walking isn't possible today, trace the circle with your eyes or your hand.
When you're back where you began, bow your head a little if it feels right, and let the circle settle with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Stupa. A mound holding relics, at the center of a path that pilgrims walk around, keeping it on their right.

orig.note: Sanskrit: stupa; in Pali, thupa. a mound built over relics.

carryVoice: Your line: walk around it. A whole visit can be one slow circle. Day eight hundred sixty-four, done.
